title: Characteristic-zero Lie containment detects factorization through a closed subgroup
statement: Let $k$ be a field of characteristic zero [def-weil-field]. Let $G,H$ be affine $k$-group schemes of finite type [def-sc-group-scheme, def-weil-finite-type-morphism], with $G$ smooth and connected [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme]. Let $K\hookrightarrow H$ be a closed subgroup scheme [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup] and $f:G\to H$ a $k$-group-scheme homomorphism. Write $\operatorname{Lie}(J)=T_{J/k,e}$ for the tangent space of any such group [def-sc-scheme-tangent-space], and regard $\operatorname{Lie}(K)$ as a subspace of $\operatorname{Lie}(H)$ by its closed immersion. If $df_e(\operatorname{Lie}(G))\subseteq\operatorname{Lie}(K)$, then $f$ factors uniquely through $K\hookrightarrow H$ as a homomorphism of $k$-group schemes. No smoothness, connectedness or normality is assumed for $K$ or $H$.

source.place: 10.14, printed p.190 (Lie preserves fibre products), Proposition 10.15, printed pp.190-191, and Cartier Theorem 3.23, printed p.71, applied to G times_H K. This factorization form is an agent-stated immediate corollary of those results, not a separate numbered theorem.

proof.text: Form $P=G\times_H K$, with projections $p:P\to G$ and $q:P\to K$. The fibre-product universal property gives $P(R)=\{(g,a):f(g)=i(a)\}$ for every commutative $k$-algebra $R$, where $i:K\hookrightarrow H$. Componentwise multiplication and inversion preserve this condition because $f,i$ are homomorphisms; the identity pair also satisfies it. These operations are morphisms by the universal property and satisfy the group diagrams after both projections, so $P$ is a group scheme and $p,q$ are homomorphisms. Base change of $i$ makes $p$ a closed immersion. Thus $P$ is affine: if $G=\operatorname{Spec}C$, then $P=\operatorname{Spec}(C/I)$ by the affine description of closed immersions. The affine finite-type algebra lemma makes $C$ finitely generated over $k$, hence the images of those generators generate $C/I$. The definition of finite type, using this single affine chart, makes $P$ finite type over $k$. In particular $p$ is a closed subgroup scheme.

source.place: 10.14 (fibre products of algebraic groups); affine closed-immersion description in Stacks 01QO and finite-type affine characterization 01T2.

proof.text: Compute the differential of $p$ directly on tangent vectors. Put $D=\operatorname{Spec}(k[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^2))$. Given $v\in T_{G/k,e_G}$, the hypothesis supplies $w\in T_{K/k,e_K}$ with $f\circ v=i\circ w$. The fibre-product universal property gives a unique $u:D\to P$ with $p\circ u=v$ and $q\circ u=w$. Its restriction to $\operatorname{Spec}k\hookrightarrow D$ is the identity pair, so $u\in T_{P/k,e_P}$ and $dp_e(u)=v$. Thus $dp_e$ is surjective. It is also injective: $i$ is injective on points over every $k$-algebra by the definition of a closed subgroup; equal $G$-projections force equal $K$-projections and hence equal maps into $P$. This is the fibre-product tangent calculation, without any smoothness assumption on $H$ or $K$.

source.place: 10.14, printed p.190, Lie preserves fibred products; here the dual-number proof is written explicitly.

proof.text: Apply Cartier smoothness to the finite-type $k$-group scheme $P$. Characteristic zero is precisely its field hypothesis, so $P$ is smooth. Now apply the smooth closed subgroup full-tangent criterion to $p:P\hookrightarrow G$: the ambient group $G$ is affine, finite type and connected by hypothesis; $P$ is smooth by Cartier; and $dp_e$ is surjective by the preceding step. It follows that $p$ is an isomorphism of group schemes over $k$.

source.place: Theorem 3.23, printed p.71, and Proposition 10.15, printed pp.190-191. Cartier also: Stacks Tag 047N, groupoids-lemma-group-scheme-characteristic-zero-smooth.

proof.text: Define $\widetilde f=q\circ p^{-1}:G\to K$. It is a homomorphism, since both projections and the inverse of the group-scheme isomorphism $p$ are homomorphisms. The fibre-product relation $i\circ q=f\circ p$ yields $i\circ\widetilde f=f$. If $h:G\to K$ is any other homomorphism with $i\circ h=f$, then $(\mathrm{id}_G,h):G\to P$ is the unique lift of that pair. Its composite with $p$ is $\mathrm{id}_G$, hence it equals $p^{-1}$, and projecting to $K$ gives $h=\widetilde f$.

source.place: 10.14-10.15, factorization corollary by the universal property of the inverse image.

proof_origin.place: Factorization corollary assembled from 10.14, Proposition 10.15 (pp.190-191), and Theorem 3.23 (p.71); explicit universal-property and dual-number arguments by Q158.
